lessons.title: Understanding Song Structure
lessons.description: Learn to identify the sections of a song and count bars.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Be able to identify intro, verse, chorus, breakdown, drop, and outro sections in any house track.

## Explanation
Every song is built from **sections** — repeating patterns of bars grouped together. In house music, the most common sections are:

- **Intro** — the opening, usually drums-only or minimal, designed for DJs to mix in
- **Breakdown** — energy drops, pads or vocals appear, percussion thins out
- **Build** — tension rises, often with risers, snare rolls, or filter sweeps
- **Drop** — the main groove hits, full energy
- **Outro** — the ending, mirrors the intro for mixing out

Most house tracks follow a predictable structure. Once you can hear it, mixing becomes much easier because you know *when* things change.

### The 4/4 Foundation
House music is in **4/4 time** — 4 beats per bar. Sections almost always land on multiples of 8 or 16 bars.

## Common Mistakes
- Confusing a breakdown with an outro
- Not counting from beat 1 — always start counting from the first kick
- Thinking every track follows the same structure (listen carefully, some tracks surprise you)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can identify intro, breakdown, build, drop, and outro in 3 different tracks
- [ ] Can count bars in groups of 4 and 8
- [ ] Can predict when a section change is coming

lessons.title: Counting Bars & Phrasing
lessons.description: Master the rhythm of dance music by counting bars and phrases.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Count bars in real-time and identify 8-bar and 16-bar phrases in house music.

## Explanation
A **bar** is 4 beats (kicks in house music). A **phrase** is a group of bars that form a musical idea — usually 8 or 16 bars.

### How to count
1. Listen for the kick drum: **1-2-3-4, 1-2-3-4**
2. Each "1-2-3-4" is one bar
3. Count bars: **1**-2-3-4, **2**-2-3-4, **3**-2-3-4, **4**-2-3-4... up to 8 or 16
4. At the end of a phrase, something changes — a new element enters, a fill happens, or the energy shifts

### Why this matters for DJing
You mix on **phrase boundaries**. If you start your incoming track on beat 1 of a new phrase in the outgoing track, the mix sounds intentional and musical.

### Phrasing trick
Most house tracks change every 16 bars. Tap your thigh on every "1" to build muscle memory.

## Common Mistakes
- Losing count when the hi-hat pattern changes
- Starting to count from the wrong beat
- Not practicing with actual music (you can't learn this from reading alone)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can count to 16 bars without losing the beat
- [ ] Can clap on the first beat of each new phrase
- [ ] Can predict section changes by counting

lessons.title: Introduction to Your DJ Software
lessons.description: Get familiar with your DJ software's interface and key features.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Navigate your DJ software confidently — load tracks, set cue points, and use the transport controls.

## Explanation
Whether you use **Rekordbox**, **Traktor**, or **Serato**, the core layout is similar:

- **Two decks** (or more) — each plays a track
- **Waveform display** — shows the audio visually
- **Mixer section** — volume faders, EQ knobs, crossfader
- **Library/browser** — where your tracks live
- **Transport controls** — play, pause, cue

### Key things to learn first
1. **Loading a track** — drag from library to a deck
2. **Play/Pause** — start and stop playback
3. **Cue button** — sets a temporary start point, press to jump back
4. **Tempo slider** — speeds up or slows down the track
5. **Waveform zoom** — zoom in to see beats clearly

### Setting up
- Import your music library
- Analyze all tracks (this detects BPM and creates waveforms)
- Set your audio output (speakers on master, headphones on cue)

## Common Mistakes
- Not analyzing tracks before a session
- Having audio routing wrong (no sound in headphones)
- Trying to learn everything at once — focus on loading and playing first

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can load a track onto each deck
- [ ] Can play, pause, and cue a track
- [ ] Can adjust the tempo slider
- [ ] Can see waveforms for loaded tracks

lessons.title: Cueing & Headphone Monitoring
lessons.description: Learn to preview tracks in your headphones before the audience hears them.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Use cue/headphone monitoring to preview and prepare the next track before mixing it in.

## Explanation
The **cue system** is how DJs listen to the next track privately while the current track plays through the speakers.

### How it works
- **Master output** → goes to speakers (what the audience hears)
- **Cue/headphone output** → goes to your headphones (what only you hear)
- **Cue buttons** on the mixer let you select which deck goes to your headphones

### Split cue vs. blend
- **Split cue**: Left ear = cue (next track), right ear = master (current track). Great for beatmatching.
- **Blend**: Both cue and master in both ears, with a knob to mix between them.

### Workflow
1. Track A is playing on master
2. Load Track B on the other deck
3. Press the cue button for Track B's channel
4. Put one headphone cup on your ear
5. Use the cue to find the first beat, set a cue point
6. When ready, start Track B and begin your mix

## Common Mistakes
- Forgetting to turn off cue after mixing in (you'll hear both tracks in headphones)
- Cue volume too loud — protect your ears
- Not setting a cue point before starting the mix

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can route audio to headphones using cue buttons
- [ ] Can use split cue to hear both tracks
- [ ] Can set and recall cue points
- [ ] Can preview a track without the audience hearing it

lessons.title: Beatmatching by Ear
lessons.description: Align the tempo and phase of two tracks using your ears.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Manually match the BPM and phase of two tracks so they play in sync.

## Explanation
Beatmatching is the core DJ skill. You're making two tracks play at the **same speed** and **same phase** (kicks landing together).

### Step by step
1. Track A is playing. Note its BPM.
2. Load Track B. Adjust its tempo slider to roughly match Track A's BPM.
3. Cue Track B in your headphones. Listen to both tracks.
4. If Track B is **faster** — you'll hear its kicks creeping ahead. Slow it down slightly.
5. If Track B is **slower** — its kicks will drift behind. Speed it up slightly.
6. Once BPMs match, you may need to **nudge** Track B forward or backward to align the phase (kicks hitting at the same time).

### How to nudge
- **Jog wheel forward** = push the track ahead slightly
- **Jog wheel backward** = pull the track back slightly
- Make tiny adjustments. Less is more.

### Listening technique
When beats are close but not matched, you'll hear a "flamming" sound — two kicks slightly apart. Adjust until they merge into one clean kick.

## Common Mistakes
- Making tempo adjustments too large — use small increments (0.1–0.5 BPM)
- Confusing tempo mismatch with phase mismatch
- Giving up too quickly — this takes hours of practice

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can match BPMs of two tracks within 0.5 BPM
- [ ] Can align the phase so kicks sound like one
- [ ] Can maintain the match for 30+ seconds

lessons.title: Using Sync & When Not To
lessons.description: Understand the sync button as a tool, and know when to rely on your ears instead.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Understand what sync does, when it helps, and why you should still learn to beatmatch manually.

## Explanation
The **sync button** automatically matches the BPM and phase of two tracks. It's a legitimate tool used by professional DJs.

### When sync is useful
- When you want to focus on creative mixing (FX, looping, layering)
- During complex 3-4 deck sets
- When BPMs are very close and you want precision
- Live situations where you need speed

### When NOT to rely on sync
- When tracks have variable BPM (older tracks, live recordings)
- When sync misreads the downbeat (it happens)
- When you haven't developed your ear yet — you won't know if something's wrong

### The golden rule
**Learn to beatmatch by ear first.** Then use sync as a tool, not a crutch. If sync fails mid-set, you need to be able to fix it manually.

### How sync can mislead
Sync locks to detected BPM grids. If a track's grid is slightly off, sync will lock to the wrong beat. You need trained ears to catch this.

## Common Mistakes
- Never learning to beatmatch because sync "works fine"
- Blindly trusting sync on every track without listening
- Feeling shame about using sync — it's a tool, use it wisely

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can explain what sync does technically
- [ ] Can identify when sync has locked to the wrong beat
- [ ] Can mix a 3-track sequence with sync off
- [ ] Can mix a 3-track sequence with sync on and understand the difference

lessons.title: Gain Staging & Volume Control
lessons.description: Set proper levels to keep your mix clean and loud without distortion.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Set gain and volume levels so your mix sounds clean, consistent, and never clips.

## Explanation
Gain staging is about controlling volume at every point in the signal chain.

### The signal chain
1. **Track gain/trim** — sets the input level for each track
2. **Channel fader** — controls volume of each channel
3. **Master output** — the final volume going to speakers

### Key rules
- **Gain/trim** should be set so the track peaks around 0dB on the channel meter (yellow zone)
- **Never hit red** — red means clipping (distortion)
- **Channel faders** should sit around 70-80% (gives you headroom)
- **Master** should peak just below 0dB

### Matching levels
Before mixing Track B in, use your headphones to compare its volume to Track A. Adjust Track B's gain until they feel equally loud. This way, when you bring the fader up, the volume stays consistent.

### Loudness vs. quality
Louder isn't better if it's distorted. A clean, well-gained mix at moderate volume sounds far better than a clipping mess at max volume.

## Common Mistakes
- Running everything in the red
- Not adjusting gain per track (every track is mastered differently)
- Pushing the master fader instead of fixing individual gains

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can set gain so meters peak at 0dB (yellow, not red)
- [ ] Can match the perceived loudness of two tracks
- [ ] Master output never clips during a transition

lessons.title: EQ Fundamentals
lessons.description: Understand the 3-band EQ and how to use it for clean mixes.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Use the 3-band EQ (Low, Mid, High) to create space for two tracks playing simultaneously.

## Explanation
The EQ (equalizer) lets you control three frequency ranges independently:

- **Low (Bass)** — kick drums, basslines (below ~250Hz)
- **Mid** — vocals, synths, melodies (~250Hz – 4kHz)
- **High (Treble)** — hi-hats, cymbals, air (above ~4kHz)

### Why EQ matters for DJing
When two tracks play at the same time, their bass frequencies **stack** and cause muddiness or distortion. The EQ lets you carve out space.

### Basic EQ mixing technique
1. Track A playing at full EQ
2. Before bringing Track B in, cut Track B's **bass to zero**
3. Bring Track B's volume up — you'll hear its highs and mids blending with Track A
4. When ready to transition, swap the bass: cut Track A's bass while bringing Track B's bass back up
5. This is the foundation of the "bass swap" transition

### The 12 o'clock rule
EQ knobs at 12 o'clock = flat (no boost or cut). Cutting is almost always better than boosting.

## Common Mistakes
- Boosting EQ instead of cutting — this adds distortion
- Having two basslines playing at full volume simultaneously
- Forgetting to reset EQ after a transition

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can identify what Low, Mid, and High control
- [ ] Can cut bass on an incoming track before blending
- [ ] Can perform a basic bass swap between two tracks
- [ ] EQ knobs return to 12 o'clock after each transition

lessons.title: Your First Transition: The Cut
lessons.description: Execute a clean, sharp transition by cutting one track to another.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Perform a clean cut transition between two tracks on a phrase boundary.

## Explanation
The **cut** is the simplest transition: you stop one track and start another at the exact same moment. It's sharp, energetic, and effective.

### How to do it
1. Track A is playing
2. Track B is cued, beatmatched, and ready on the first beat
3. Count Track A's phrases — wait for a phrase boundary (end of a 16-bar section)
4. On beat 1 of the new phrase: **drop Track A's volume to zero** and **push Track B's volume up** simultaneously
5. Done. Track B is now playing.

### When to use cuts
- High-energy moments
- Between tracks with very different feels
- When you want a dramatic change
- Drops and build-ups

### Making it clean
- The cut MUST happen on beat 1 of a phrase
- Both tracks must be at the same BPM
- Track B's cue point must be set on its beat 1

## Common Mistakes
- Cutting off-phrase (sounds jarring and unintentional)
- Not having Track B beatmatched (BPM mismatch is obvious)
- Cutting during a vocal or melodic phrase in Track A

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can execute a cut that lands on beat 1 of a phrase
- [ ] The transition sounds intentional, not accidental
- [ ] No gap or overlap — it's one clean moment

lessons.title: Your First Transition: The Fade
lessons.description: Execute a smooth fade transition using volume and crossfader.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Perform a smooth fade transition where one track gradually replaces another.

## Explanation
The **fade** is a gentle transition: you slowly reduce Track A's volume while increasing Track B's. Both tracks play simultaneously during the blend.

### How to do it
1. Track A is playing
2. Track B is cued and beatmatched
3. On a phrase boundary, start Track B with its fader low
4. Over the next 16–32 bars, gradually bring Track B's fader up
5. Simultaneously, gradually bring Track A's fader down
6. When Track B is at full volume and Track A is silent, the transition is complete

### Using EQ during a fade
For a cleaner fade:
- Cut Track B's bass as you bring it in
- Swap the bass halfway through the fade
- This prevents bass muddiness during the blend

### Crossfader vs. channel faders
- **Channel faders**: More control, adjust each track independently
- **Crossfader**: One control that blends between decks — faster but less nuance

## Common Mistakes
- Fading too quickly (sounds rushed) or too slowly (crowd loses interest)
- Not using EQ during the fade (bass mud)
- Starting the fade at a random point instead of a phrase boundary

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can execute a 16-bar fade that sounds smooth
- [ ] Can execute a 32-bar fade
- [ ] Can use EQ during the fade to keep bass clean
- [ ] Transition starts and ends on phrase boundaries

lessons.title: Recording & Reviewing Your Mixes
lessons.description: Record your practice mixes and learn to self-critique effectively.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Record a practice mix and review it critically to identify areas for improvement.

## Explanation
Recording yourself is the fastest way to improve. When you're mixing live, you're focused on the next move. Listening back lets you hear what the audience hears.

### How to record
- Most DJ software has a built-in recording function
- **Rekordbox**: Settings → Recording → choose a save location
- **Traktor**: Preferences → Recording → enable
- **Serato**: Click the record button in the top bar
- Save as WAV or high-quality MP3 (320kbps)

### How to review
1. Listen to the full mix the next day (fresh ears)
2. Take notes on each transition:
   - Was it on-phrase?
   - Was the beatmatching clean?
   - Was there bass mud?
   - Did the energy flow make sense?
3. Rate each transition: Clean / OK / Needs Work
4. Note the timestamp of transitions that need improvement
5. Practice those specific transitions again

### Building a review habit
- Record every practice session
- Review at least once a week
- Keep a practice log (use the Practice Log feature in DJ Lab!)

## Common Mistakes
- Never listening back to recordings
- Being too harsh on yourself early on — progress takes time
- Not noting specific timestamps (vague feedback doesn't help)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can record a mix in your DJ software
- [ ] Have listened back to a recording and taken notes
- [ ] Have identified at least 3 specific things to improve
- [ ] Have logged the session in your practice log

lessons.title: House Music Structure Deep Dive
lessons.description: Understand the specific structural conventions of house and tech house tracks.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Identify the standard structure of house and tech house tracks and use that knowledge for mixing.

## Explanation
House tracks have **predictable structures** designed for DJs. Understanding these patterns lets you plan transitions.

### Typical house/tech house structure
```
Intro (16-32 bars) → Build (8-16 bars) → Drop 1 (32 bars)
→ Breakdown (16-32 bars) → Build (8-16 bars) → Drop 2 (32 bars)
→ Outro (16-32 bars)
```

### Key characteristics by section
- **Intro**: Drums only or minimal elements. This is your **mix-in point**.
- **Build**: Energy rises — risers, snare rolls, filter sweeps
- **Drop**: Full groove — kick, bass, hats, synths, everything
- **Breakdown**: Drums thin out, pads/vocals take over, tension builds
- **Outro**: Mirrors the intro. This is your **mix-out point**.

### Tech house specifics
- Intros/outros tend to be longer (32 bars)
- Breakdowns are shorter and less dramatic than progressive house
- More percussion-driven, fewer melodic breakdowns
- Groove is king — the drop is about the rhythm, not a "big moment"

### Mix points
The standard approach: mix the **intro** of Track B over the **outro** of Track A. These sections are designed to overlap.

## Common Mistakes
- Trying to mix during a breakdown (elements clash)
- Not recognizing the difference between a tech house drop and a big-room drop
- Ignoring the outro and cutting too early

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can map out the structure of 3 tech house tracks
- [ ] Can identify intro/outro mix points in each track
- [ ] Understand how tech house structure differs from other house subgenres

lessons.title: EQ Mixing: The Bass Swap
lessons.description: Master the bass swap technique for clean house music transitions.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Perform a seamless bass swap transition between two house tracks.

## Explanation
The **bass swap** is the bread-and-butter transition for house and tech house DJs. You swap the bass from the outgoing track to the incoming track in one clean move.

### Step by step
1. Track A is playing (full EQ)
2. Track B is cued, beatmatched, bass EQ **killed** (turned all the way down)
3. Bring Track B in with fader up — you'll hear its highs and mids over Track A
4. Blend for 8-16 bars, letting the tracks overlap
5. On a phrase boundary: **simultaneously** bring Track B's bass up to full and cut Track A's bass to zero
6. The bass instantly transfers from A to B
7. Over the next 8-16 bars, fade Track A out completely

### The swap moment
This should happen on **beat 1 of a new phrase**. Do it quickly — it's not a gradual move, it's a decisive swap.

### Advanced: partial bass swap
Instead of full kill, try reducing Track A's bass to 30% while bringing Track B's to 70%. This creates a softer transition.

## Common Mistakes
- Swapping off-phrase (sounds random)
- Having both basses at full volume at the same time (instant mud)
- Forgetting to bring Track A's bass back to 12 o'clock after transition

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can execute a clean bass swap on a phrase boundary
- [ ] No bass mud during the transition
- [ ] The swap feels intentional and musical
- [ ] Can do 5 bass swaps in a row without mistakes

lessons.title: Using Loops for Mixing
lessons.description: Use loops to extend mix points and create longer, smoother transitions.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Loop intros, outros, or specific sections to create flexible mix points.

## Explanation
Loops let you **repeat a section** of a track indefinitely. This is hugely useful for mixing because not every track has a long enough intro or outro.

### Common loop uses
- **Loop the intro** of the incoming track while you wait for the right moment to bring it in
- **Loop the outro** of the outgoing track to extend your mix time
- **Loop a drum section** to create a percussion bed for transitions

### How to loop
1. Set a loop start point (usually 4, 8, or 16 bars)
2. The software will repeat that section
3. When you're ready, press the loop button again to exit — the track continues playing

### Loop lengths for house
- **4 bars**: Tight, rhythmic loops (good for drum sections)
- **8 bars**: Most common for mixing (a full phrase)
- **16 bars**: Extended blends, gives you plenty of time

### Creative looping
- Loop a vocal chop or riff from Track A while Track B plays
- Loop Track B's buildup to extend the tension
- Use loop + EQ together for maximum control

## Common Mistakes
- Looping at a non-musical length (2 bars can sound choppy)
- Forgetting to exit the loop (track never progresses)
- Looping a section with a riser or build (sounds weird when it resets)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can set a clean 8-bar loop on an intro
- [ ] Can use a loop to extend a mix point
- [ ] Can exit a loop on a phrase boundary
- [ ] Can mix using loops on both decks

lessons.title: Filter Transitions
lessons.description: Use high-pass and low-pass filters to create smooth, frequency-based transitions.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Use filter sweeps to blend tracks by gradually removing or adding frequencies.

## Explanation
Filters are like EQ but more dramatic. Instead of cutting one band, a filter removes everything above or below a cutoff point.

- **High-pass filter (HPF)**: Removes low frequencies. Track sounds thin and airy.
- **Low-pass filter (LPF)**: Removes high frequencies. Track sounds muffled and warm.

### Filter transition technique
1. Track A is playing clean
2. Track B is cued and ready (full volume, filter fully open)
3. Apply a **high-pass filter** to Track A — gradually sweep it up over 16 bars
4. Track A loses its bass and body, becoming thin
5. Meanwhile, bring Track B in underneath
6. On a phrase boundary, kill Track A and open Track B fully

### Reverse approach
- Bring Track B in with a **low-pass filter** (sounds muffled)
- Gradually open the filter over 16-32 bars
- The track "reveals itself" as the filter opens

### Filter + EQ combo
You can use filter on one deck and EQ on the other for layered control. Very effective for tech house.

## Common Mistakes
- Sweeping the filter too fast (sounds like a DJ mistake, not a transition)
- Using filter on a track with prominent vocals (sounds unnatural)
- Not combining filter with volume — filter alone doesn't complete a transition

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can perform a high-pass filter sweep on the outgoing track
- [ ] Can bring in a track using a low-pass filter reveal
- [ ] Filter sweeps are smooth and musical, not abrupt
- [ ] Can combine filter with EQ in a single transition

lessons.title: Energy Management
lessons.description: Learn to read and control the energy arc of a DJ set.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Plan and execute a set with intentional energy flow — building up, sustaining, and releasing tension.

## Explanation
A great DJ set tells a story. It's not just about playing good tracks — it's about controlling **energy over time**.

### The energy arc
Think of your set as a wave:
```
Opening (low energy) → Build → Peak → Sustain → Cooldown → Build again → Final peak → Wind down
```

### Energy factors
- **BPM**: Higher BPM = more energy (but don't jump more than 2-3 BPM between tracks)
- **Bass heaviness**: Deeper, heavier bass = more energy
- **Percussion density**: More layers = more drive
- **Vocals**: Vocals grab attention, good for peaks
- **Breakdowns**: Brief energy dips that make the next drop feel bigger

### Planning your energy
- Open with stripped-back, groove-focused tracks
- Build energy over the first 20-30 minutes
- Hit your peak around 60-75% into the set
- Use breakdowns strategically — don't overspam them
- Wind down the last 2-3 tracks

### Reading the room (for live sets)
- Watch for dancing, head-nodding, hands-up
- If people are looking at phones or talking, energy might be too low
- If people look tired, you may have peaked too early

## Common Mistakes
- Starting at full energy (nowhere to go but down)
- Every track being a banger (no dynamics, gets tiring)
- Ignoring the crowd's response

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can categorize your tracks by energy level (1-5 scale)
- [ ] Can plan a 30-minute set with an intentional energy arc
- [ ] The set doesn't feel flat or monotonous

lessons.title: Track Selection & Library Building
lessons.description: Curate, organize, and tag your music library for efficient DJing.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Build a well-organized DJ library with tracks tagged by BPM, key, energy, and genre.

## Explanation
Your **library** is your instrument. A well-organized library lets you find the right track in seconds.

### Where to find music
- **Beatport** — the standard for house/tech house
- **Bandcamp** — independent releases, great for unique finds
- **Traxsource** — deep house, soulful house, classic vibes
- **SoundCloud** — unreleased edits, DJ tools, promos
- **DJ record pools** — subscription services with curated selections

### What to buy
- Focus on **house and tech house** initially
- Build a core library of 50-100 tracks before expanding
- Include a mix of: bangers, groovers, openers, closers, tools (percussion-only tracks)

### Organization system
Tag every track with:
1. **BPM** (auto-detected but verify)
2. **Key** (for harmonic mixing later)
3. **Energy level** (1-5)
4. **Vibe/mood** (groovy, dark, vocal, driving, melodic)
5. **Mix points** (set cue points for intro, drop, outro)

### Playlists
- Create playlists by energy level or vibe
- Make a "Set Starters" and "Set Closers" playlist
- Keep a "Need to Practice" playlist for new tracks

## Common Mistakes
- Downloading hundreds of tracks without listening to them
- Not tagging or organizing (can't find anything mid-set)
- Only buying trending tracks (your sets will sound like everyone else's)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have 30+ tracks organized with BPM and energy tags
- [ ] Have at least 3 playlists (openers, peak, closers)
- [ ] Have cue points set on all tracks in your main playlist
- [ ] Can find any track in under 10 seconds

lessons.title: Building a 30-Minute Mix
lessons.description: Plan and execute a complete 30-minute DJ set from start to finish.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Prepare and record a 30-minute mix with intentional track selection, energy flow, and clean transitions.

## Explanation
A 30-minute mix is the perfect practice format. It's long enough to develop a flow but short enough to review and improve.

### Planning the set
1. Pick 8-10 tracks (you won't use all of them)
2. Arrange them by energy: low → medium → high → medium
3. Check BPM compatibility (stay within 2-3 BPM range)
4. Check key compatibility where possible (Camelot wheel)
5. Note your transition plan for each pair

### Set outline template
```
Track 1 (opener, 124 BPM, low energy) — 3 min
  → bass swap into Track 2
Track 2 (groover, 125 BPM, medium energy) — 3 min
  → filter transition into Track 3
Track 3 (builder, 125 BPM, medium-high energy) — 3 min
  → loop + bass swap into Track 4
...
```

### The recording session
1. Set up your mix plan on paper
2. Hit record
3. Play through the set
4. If a transition goes wrong, keep going — don't restart
5. Review the recording and note improvements

### After recording
- Listen back the next day
- Note each transition quality
- Identify the weakest transition and practice it 5 times
- Re-record the full mix with improvements

## Common Mistakes
- Over-preparing (scripting every second — leave room for instinct)
- Restarting after every mistake (you need to practice recovery)
- Not recording (you lose the ability to review)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have a written set plan with 8-10 tracks
- [ ] Have recorded the full 30-minute mix
- [ ] Have reviewed the recording and noted improvements
- [ ] Transitions are mostly on-phrase with clean bass management

lessons.title: Advanced Transitions: Echo & Reverb
lessons.description: Use echo and reverb effects to create atmospheric transitions.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Use echo (delay) and reverb effects to create smooth, atmospheric transitions between tracks.

## Explanation
FX-based transitions add polish and creativity to your mixing. Echo and reverb are the most DJ-friendly effects.

### Echo (Delay) transition
1. Track A is playing
2. Assign echo effect to Track A's channel
3. Set echo time to match the beat (1/2 or 3/4 works well for house)
4. At a phrase boundary, activate echo and gradually reduce Track A's volume
5. The echo tails off naturally as Track B takes over
6. The effect: Track A "echoes away" into the distance

### Reverb transition
1. Track A is playing
2. Assign reverb to Track A's channel
3. At a phrase boundary, increase reverb wet/dry toward fully wet
4. Track A becomes a wash of reverb
5. Bring Track B in underneath the reverb wash
6. Cut Track A — the reverb tail bridges the gap

### Combining FX
- Echo + high-pass filter = track echoes away and gets thinner
- Reverb + volume reduction = atmospheric fade
- Use FX sparingly — they're seasoning, not the main dish

### Timing FX
Sync your echo time to the BPM for musical results. Most DJ software has a sync button for FX.

## Common Mistakes
- Using too much echo (sounds washy and uncontrolled)
- Not beat-syncing the delay time (off-beat echoes sound wrong)
- Leaving effects on after the transition (next track sounds weird)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can perform an echo-out transition
- [ ] Can perform a reverb wash transition
- [ ] Effects are beat-synced and musical
- [ ] Effects are turned off after each transition

lessons.title: Harmonic Mixing Basics
lessons.description: Use musical keys to create harmonically pleasing transitions.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Use the Camelot Wheel to mix tracks in compatible keys for smoother-sounding blends.

## Explanation
Harmonic mixing means blending tracks that are in **compatible musical keys**. When keys clash, the blend sounds dissonant. When they match, it sounds musical.

### The Camelot Wheel
The Camelot system assigns every musical key a number (1-12) and letter (A or B):
- **A** = minor key
- **B** = major key
- Numbers represent the key position

### Compatible keys
From any position, you can mix to:
- **Same number** (e.g., 5A → 5A) — same key, always works
- **+1 or -1** (e.g., 5A → 6A or 4A) — adjacent keys, smooth
- **Same number, opposite letter** (e.g., 5A → 5B) — relative major/minor

Example: If Track A is 8A (Am), compatible tracks are 7A, 8A, 9A, or 8B.

### Practical workflow
1. Analyze all your tracks' keys (most DJ software does this)
2. Tag tracks with Camelot codes
3. When selecting the next track, check that it's within 1 step on the Camelot wheel
4. Not every transition needs to be harmonic — cuts don't blend harmonically anyway

### When it matters most
Harmonic mixing is most important during **long blends** where both tracks' melodies or basslines play simultaneously.

## Common Mistakes
- Obsessing over key matching at the expense of energy flow
- Trusting auto-key detection blindly (it's wrong ~20% of the time)
- Only mixing same-key tracks (limits your options)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Understand the Camelot Wheel
- [ ] Can identify compatible keys for any Camelot code
- [ ] Have tagged at least 20 tracks with their keys
- [ ] Can hear the difference between a key-matched and key-clashed blend

lessons.title: Playing Live: Prep & Mindset
lessons.description: Prepare for your first live set with practical tips and mental strategies.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Be prepared for a live DJ set — technically, mentally, and practically.

## Explanation
Playing live is different from bedroom practice. Here's how to prepare.

### Technical prep
- **USB drives**: Prepare two USB sticks with your library (one backup)
- **Laptop backup**: If using laptop, have charger and backup audio cable
- **Track selection**: Prepare 2-3x more tracks than you need
- **Playlists**: Organize by energy level and vibe
- **Test your files**: Make sure they play without errors

### Before the set
- Arrive early and check the equipment
- Ask the previous DJ about their BPM and energy level
- Set your gain levels with the first track before going live
- Have your first 3 tracks planned

### During the set
- **Stay calm** — mistakes happen, keep going
- **Don't look at your phone** — you're performing
- **Watch the crowd** — adjust energy based on their response
- **Use simple transitions first** — nail the basics before getting fancy
- **Have a recovery plan** — if a mix goes wrong, cut to the safe track

### Mindset
- You're a guide, not a jukebox. Play for the room.
- One bad transition won't ruin a set. People forget in 30 seconds.
- Confidence comes from preparation. Practice more, stress less.
- Have fun. If you're enjoying it, the crowd will too.

## Common Mistakes
- Not checking equipment before starting
- Playing only for yourself instead of reading the room
- Panicking after a mistake and making it worse
- Over-planning every transition (be ready to adapt)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have two prepared USB drives with organized playlists
- [ ] Have a loose plan for first 3 tracks
- [ ] Have a recovery strategy for bad transitions
- [ ] Can play a 30-minute practice set without stopping after mistakes

lessons.title: DAW Introduction
lessons.description: Set up and navigate your Digital Audio Workstation for music production.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Set up a DAW (Ableton Live, Logic Pro, or FL Studio) and understand the basic interface.

## Explanation
A **DAW** (Digital Audio Workstation) is your production studio. It's where you arrange, record, edit, and mix music.

### Choosing a DAW
- **Ableton Live** — most popular for electronic music. Session View + Arrangement View. Highly recommended for house/tech house.
- **Logic Pro** — Mac only. Great stock plugins. Used by many professionals.
- **FL Studio** — Pattern-based workflow. Strong for beginners. Cross-platform.

### Core concepts (universal)
1. **Tracks/Channels**: Each instrument or sound gets its own track
2. **Timeline/Arrangement**: Where you arrange your song left to right
3. **Mixer**: Volume, pan, and effects for each track
4. **Transport**: Play, stop, record, BPM setting
5. **Browser**: Where you find sounds, samples, and plugins

### First session setup
1. Create a new project
2. Set BPM to 124-126 (standard tech house range)
3. Set time signature to 4/4
4. Create a few tracks: drums, bass, synth
5. Familiarize yourself with zoom, scroll, and track controls

### Save often
Save your project immediately and keep saving. Use "Save As" for versions.

## Common Mistakes
- Spending weeks comparing DAWs instead of picking one and starting
- Not learning keyboard shortcuts (they save massive time)
- Opening a project without setting BPM first

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have a DAW installed and running
- [ ] Can create a new project and set BPM
- [ ] Can create tracks and load instruments/samples
- [ ] Can play, stop, and navigate the timeline
- [ ] Have saved a project file

lessons.title: The 4-on-the-Floor Kick
lessons.description: Program the fundamental kick pattern that drives all house music.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Program a solid 4-on-the-floor kick pattern that sounds like professional house music.

## Explanation
The **4-on-the-floor** kick is the heartbeat of house music: a kick drum on every beat.

```
Beat:  1   2   3   4   1   2   3   4
Kick:  X   X   X   X   X   X   X   X
```

### Choosing a kick sample
For house/tech house, your kick should be:
- **Punchy** with a clear transient (the initial click)
- **Sub-bass weight** (the low-end boom)
- Medium-long tail (not too short, not too boomy)
- Listen to reference tracks and find a similar kick

### Programming the pattern
1. Create a drum rack or sampler track
2. Load your kick sample
3. Place kicks on every quarter note (beats 1, 2, 3, 4)
4. Set velocity consistently (around 100-110 out of 127)
5. Listen. It should sound steady and powerful.

### Tuning
- Most house kicks sit around **45-55 Hz** fundamental
- Tune your kick to match your song's key for a cleaner low end
- Use a tuner plugin or your ears

### Making it feel right
- The kick should feel like it's pulling you forward
- If it feels flat, try a slight velocity accent on beat 1
- A/B with reference tracks constantly

## Common Mistakes
- Using a kick that's too boomy or too thin
- Velocity too high (sounds robotic) or too varied (sounds inconsistent)
- Not checking mono compatibility (bass should sound good in mono)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have a clean 4-on-the-floor kick pattern
- [ ] Kick sounds punchy and sits in the right frequency range
- [ ] Pattern loops cleanly with no clicks or pops
- [ ] Sounds good on headphones and speakers

lessons.title: Hi-Hats & Percussion
lessons.description: Build a percussion layer with hi-hats, claps, shakers, and rides.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Program a complete percussion pattern with hi-hats, claps, and supporting percussion.

## Explanation
Percussion gives house music its groove and forward motion. Beyond the kick, you need hi-hats, claps/snares, and supporting elements.

### Hi-hat patterns
**Closed hi-hat** — the most common pattern:
```
Beat:    1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &
Hi-hat:  . X . X . X . X    (offbeat / upbeat)
```
This offbeat pattern is classic house. The hats fall between the kicks.

**Open hi-hat** accent:
```
Beat:    1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &
Open HH: . . . . . . . X    (end of bar, adds lift)
```

### Clap / Snare
Place on beats **2 and 4** (the backbeat):
```
Beat:  1   2   3   4
Clap:  .   X   .   X
```

### Supporting percussion
Add texture with:
- **Shakers**: 16th notes at low volume for drive
- **Ride cymbal**: Subtle, adds shimmer
- **Rimshots/toms**: Occasional accent hits
- **Congas/bongos**: Adds a human feel

### Layering tips
- Start with kick + hi-hat + clap as your foundation
- Add one element at a time
- Less is more — if it grooves, don't add more
- Pan percussion elements slightly for width

## Common Mistakes
- Too many percussion elements (sounds cluttered)
- Hi-hats too loud (should sit behind the kick)
- No velocity variation (sounds robotic)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have a kick + hi-hat + clap pattern that grooves
- [ ] Hi-hats have subtle velocity variation
- [ ] Can add and remove elements without losing the groove
- [ ] Pattern sounds like house music when played alongside a reference

lessons.title: Creating Groove & Swing
lessons.description: Add swing and micro-timing adjustments to make your drums feel alive.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Apply swing and micro-timing to make programmed drums feel human and groovy.

## Explanation
Perfectly quantized drums sound stiff. Real house music has **groove** — subtle timing variations that make it feel alive.

### What is swing?
Swing shifts every **offbeat** note slightly late. Instead of perfectly even 8th notes, the offbeats are pushed forward, creating a "shuffle" feel.

- **0% swing** = straight, robotic
- **50-60% swing** = subtle groove (common in house)
- **66% swing** = triplet feel (too much for most house)

### How to add swing
1. In your DAW, find the groove/swing setting
2. Apply 50-55% swing to your hi-hats and percussion
3. Keep the **kick straight** (no swing on the kick)
4. Listen. The hi-hats should feel like they're slightly "leaning" into the beat.

### Micro-timing
Beyond swing, manually nudge individual hits:
- Push a snare 5-10ms late for a **laid-back** feel
- Pull a hi-hat 5ms early for a **pushing** feel
- Add random velocity variation (±10-15%) for human feel

### Groove templates
Many DAWs include groove templates extracted from classic drum machines (MPC, 808, 909). Try applying an MPC groove to your hats.

### A/B testing
Record two versions — one straight, one with groove. Listen to both. The groovy version should make you nod your head more.

## Common Mistakes
- Adding too much swing (sounds drunk, not groovy)
- Applying swing to the kick (destabilizes the foundation)
- Not listening back — groove is a feeling, not a number

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can apply swing to hi-hats and percussion
- [ ] Drums feel more alive than the quantized version
- [ ] Kick remains straight and stable
- [ ] Can identify the difference between groovy and stiff drums

lessons.title: Kick & Bass Relationship
lessons.description: Get your kick and bass working together without fighting.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Make the kick and bass coexist cleanly in the low end of your mix.

## Explanation
The kick and bass are both low-frequency elements. If they're not managed properly, they'll fight for space and make your mix sound muddy.

### The fundamental rule
Kick and bass should **not play at the same time at full volume**. One should dominate at any given moment.

### Technique 1: Sidechain compression
The most common approach in house music:
1. Put a compressor on your bass track
2. Set the kick as the sidechain input
3. Every time the kick hits, the bass ducks briefly
4. The kick punches through, then the bass swells back
5. This creates the classic "pumping" feel of house music

### Settings guide
- **Threshold**: Low enough that the kick triggers compression
- **Ratio**: 4:1 to 8:1
- **Attack**: Fast (0-5ms)
- **Release**: Adjust to taste (50-150ms for house). The bass should return by the next 8th note.

### Technique 2: Frequency separation
- EQ the kick to dominate 50-80Hz (sub)
- EQ the bass to sit above 80Hz (low-mid)
- They occupy different frequency spaces

### Technique 3: Pattern separation
- Write the bass pattern to avoid the kick hits
- Bass notes play between kicks
- Common in tech house — offbeat basslines

## Common Mistakes
- Sidechain too aggressive (bass disappears completely)
- No sidechain at all (muddy low end)
- Kick and bass in different keys (dissonant low end)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can set up sidechain compression on bass from kick
- [ ] Low end sounds clean and punchy
- [ ] Can hear both kick and bass clearly
- [ ] Sidechain has the right release time for the groove

lessons.title: Bass Design for House Music
lessons.description: Create rolling, driving basslines typical of house and tech house.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Design and program basslines that drive your house tracks forward.

## Explanation
The bassline is the engine of house music. It provides momentum, groove, and harmonic foundation.

### Types of house basslines
1. **Rolling bass**: Repeating 8th or 16th note pattern, filter modulation. Classic tech house.
2. **Stab bass**: Short, punchy hits on specific beats. Minimal house.
3. **Sub bass**: Deep, sustained notes. Deep house.
4. **Acid bass**: 303-style squelchy, resonant filter. Acid house/tech house.

### Creating a rolling bass
1. Use a synth (Operator, Serum, or a simple saw/square oscillator)
2. Set it to a **saw wave** or **square wave**
3. Add a **low-pass filter** with moderate resonance
4. Add **filter envelope**: short attack, medium decay, low sustain
5. Program a repeating 8th-note pattern
6. Each note triggers the filter envelope, creating the "roll"

### The tech house bassline formula
- Key: usually minor (Am, Gm, Dm are common)
- Pattern: 8th notes with some variation
- Filter: automate cutoff for movement
- Keep it **mono** (bass should be centered)

### Layering
- Layer a sub (sine wave, low octave) with a mid-bass (saw, higher octave)
- Sub provides weight, mid-bass provides character
- High-pass the mid-bass around 100Hz so it doesn't clash with the sub

## Common Mistakes
- Bass too wide (should be mono below 200Hz)
- Too many notes (keep it simple and repetitive)
- Not sidechaining to the kick

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can create a rolling bass patch from a basic synth
- [ ] Bassline grooves with the drum pattern
- [ ] Bass is in mono and doesn't clash with the kick
- [ ] Can hear the filter movement adding character

lessons.title: Arrangement: Intro to Outro
lessons.description: Structure a full house track from intro through outro.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Arrange a full house track with proper intro, build, drop, breakdown, and outro sections.

## Explanation
Arrangement is how you turn an 8-bar loop into a full track. House arrangement follows conventions that DJs rely on.

### Standard house arrangement (4-6 minutes)
```
Intro (16-32 bars) — drums only, for DJ mixing
Build (8-16 bars) — elements enter gradually
Drop 1 (32 bars) — full groove, all elements
Breakdown (16-32 bars) — strip back, introduce new element
Build (8-16 bars) — tension rises
Drop 2 (32 bars) — full groove returns (maybe with variation)
Outro (16-32 bars) — elements exit, mirrors intro
```

### Key principles
1. **Add/remove one element at a time** — don't dump everything in at once
2. **16 bars minimum** for any section — shorter feels rushed
3. **Intro and outro mirror each other** — DJs need drums-only sections
4. **The breakdown is the emotional center** — this is where vocals, pads, or new melodies appear
5. **Drop 2 should be slightly different** from Drop 1 (add a new percussion element, extra synth layer)

### Building tension
- Use **risers** (noise sweeps going up) before drops
- Use **snare rolls** accelerating into the drop
- **Filter automation** — slowly open a low-pass filter over 8 bars
- **Remove the kick** for 4-8 bars before the drop (makes the return feel bigger)

### DJ-friendly arrangement
- First 16 bars: kick only or kick + hats
- Last 16 bars: same as first 16 bars
- This gives DJs clean mix points

## Common Mistakes
- Intro/outro too short (DJs can't mix it)
- Everything appears at once (no journey)
- Arrangement doesn't breathe — every bar is full

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have arranged a 4+ minute track with all sections
- [ ] Intro and outro are DJ-friendly (drums only)
- [ ] Elements enter and exit one at a time
- [ ] There's a clear breakdown and build

lessons.title: Sampling & Chopping
lessons.description: Use samples legally and creatively in your productions.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Find, chop, and use samples effectively in your house productions.

## Explanation
Sampling is a cornerstone of house music production. From classic disco chops to modern vocal stabs, samples add character.

### Where to find samples
- **Sample packs**: Splice, Loopmasters, Sample Magic (royalty-free)
- **Vinyl**: Record shops, Discogs (needs clearing for commercial release)
- **Field recordings**: Record your own sounds
- **Foley**: Everyday objects as percussion

### Legal considerations
- **Royalty-free sample packs**: Safe to use in any production
- **Sampling from existing songs**: Requires clearance for commercial release
- **Creative Commons**: Check the specific license
- **Flip test**: If someone can identify the source, you probably need clearance

### Chopping techniques
1. **Vocal chops**: Take a word or syllable from a vocal, pitch it, reverse it, layer it
2. **Drum breaks**: Isolate individual hits from a break
3. **Melodic stabs**: Grab a chord or riff, warp it, filter it
4. **Texture layers**: Ambient sounds, vinyl noise, room tone

### Processing samples
- **Time-stretch**: Match the sample to your BPM
- **Pitch-shift**: Change key to match your track
- **Reverse**: Play samples backward for risers and transitions
- **Filter**: Remove unwanted frequencies
- **Chop and rearrange**: Cut into pieces and create new patterns

## Common Mistakes
- Using samples completely unprocessed (sounds like a lazy copy)
- Not time-stretching to match BPM (sample drifts out of sync)
- Over-sampling (your track should have original elements too)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can import and time-stretch a sample to match BPM
- [ ] Can chop a vocal into usable stabs
- [ ] Can apply basic processing (filter, reverse, pitch)
- [ ] Know the difference between royalty-free and rights-managed samples

lessons.title: Compression Basics
lessons.description: Use compression to control dynamics and add punch to your mix.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Understand and apply compression to drums, bass, and full mix.

## Explanation
Compression reduces the difference between the loudest and quietest parts of a sound. It makes things punchier, more consistent, and louder.

### How a compressor works
- **Threshold**: Volume level where compression starts
- **Ratio**: How much compression is applied (2:1 = gentle, 10:1 = heavy)
- **Attack**: How quickly compression kicks in after exceeding threshold
- **Release**: How quickly compression stops after signal drops below threshold
- **Makeup gain**: Compensates for volume reduction

### Compression for house music

**Kick drum**:
- Ratio: 4:1
- Attack: Slow (10-30ms) — lets the transient through for punch
- Release: Medium (50-100ms) — resets before the next hit

**Bass**:
- Ratio: 3:1 to 4:1
- Attack: Medium (10-20ms)
- Release: Auto or medium — should follow the bass note length

**Drum bus**:
- Ratio: 2:1 to 3:1
- Attack: Slow (20-30ms) — keeps the punch
- Release: Match to the groove
- This glues the drums together

### Parallel compression
Blend the compressed signal with the uncompressed signal. You get punch AND dynamics. Many pros use this on drums.

### The gain reduction meter
Watch the gain reduction meter. For most house applications, you want 3-6dB of gain reduction. More than 10dB is usually too much.

## Common Mistakes
- Over-compressing everything (sounds flat and lifeless)
- Attack too fast on drums (kills the punch)
- Not using makeup gain (compressed track sounds quieter)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can set up a compressor with correct parameters
- [ ] Can compress a kick to be punchy without squashing
- [ ] Can apply bus compression to glue drums together
- [ ] Can hear the difference between compressed and uncompressed

lessons.title: Layering Sounds
lessons.description: Stack multiple sounds to create rich, full textures.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Layer synths and percussion to create fuller, more professional-sounding arrangements.

## Explanation
Layering is combining multiple sounds to create something richer than any single sound alone.

### Why layer?
- A single snare sample might be thin. Layer 3 snares together = fat, characterful snare.
- A single synth might lack presence. Layer a sub + mid + top = full, powerful synth.

### Percussion layering
1. **Kick layering**: Sub kick (low thump) + top kick (click/attack). High-pass the top kick around 150Hz.
2. **Snare/clap layering**: Snare sample + clap sample + noise burst. Each adds a different character.
3. **Hi-hat layering**: Closed hat + shaker at low volume. Adds texture without changing the rhythm.

### Synth layering
1. **Sub layer** (sine wave): Pure low end, mono, below 200Hz
2. **Body layer** (saw/square): Main character, mid frequencies
3. **Top layer** (bright synth or noise): Air and presence, above 5kHz

### Rules for clean layering
- **EQ each layer** to occupy its own frequency range
- **Don't duplicate frequencies** — if two layers have strong 200Hz content, cut one
- **Less is more** — 2-3 layers is usually enough
- **Phase check** — play layers together in mono. If it sounds thinner in mono, there's phase cancellation. Flip the polarity of one layer or adjust timing.

### Group processing
After layering, group the layers and process them together (compression, saturation) to glue them into one cohesive sound.

## Common Mistakes
- Too many layers (muddiness, phase issues)
- Not EQ-ing layers (frequency masking)
- Layers fighting for the same frequency space

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can layer a kick with sub + top components
- [ ] Can layer a snare/clap from 2-3 samples
- [ ] Each layer occupies its own frequency range
- [ ] Layered sounds pass the mono compatibility check

lessons.title: Tension & Release
lessons.description: Build and release tension through arrangement and FX.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Use tension-building techniques to make your drops and transitions more impactful.

## Explanation
The magic of dance music is in the **contrast** between tension and release. The drop feels powerful because the build made you wait for it.

### Tension-building tools

**Risers**:
- White noise sweep going up in pitch
- Synth note rising in pitch over 8-16 bars
- Layer multiple risers for intensity

**Snare/clap rolls**:
- Start with quarter notes, accelerate to 8ths, then 16ths, then 32nds
- Increase velocity as the roll gets faster
- Classic build technique

**Filter automation**:
- Slowly open a low-pass filter over 16 bars
- The mix gets brighter and bigger as the filter opens
- Combine with a riser for maximum effect

**Removing elements**:
- Remove the kick 8 bars before the drop
- Remove bass 4 bars before the drop
- The absence creates anticipation
- When everything returns on the drop, it hits harder

**Reverb automation**:
- Increase reverb on elements during the build
- Cut reverb instantly on the drop — sudden dryness = impact

### The release (the drop)
- Everything returns at once on beat 1
- Kick, bass, full drums, synths — maximum energy
- The contrast between the stripped build and the full drop is what creates the "moment"

### Arrangement trick
The longer the build, the bigger the drop feels. But don't overdo it — 8-16 bars is the sweet spot for house music.

## Common Mistakes
- Build too long (crowd loses interest)
- Drop doesn't feel different enough from the build
- No contrast — everything stays at the same intensity

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can create a riser that builds tension over 16 bars
- [ ] Can program an accelerating snare roll
- [ ] Can automate a filter for a gradual build
- [ ] The drop feels satisfying after the build

lessons.title: Finishing a Track
lessons.description: Basic mixdown, export, and next steps for completing a production.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Complete a track by applying basic mixdown techniques and exporting a finished file.

## Explanation
Finishing a track is one of the hardest skills in production. Here's a practical approach to getting your track across the finish line.

### Mixdown checklist

**1. Level balance**
- Kick should be the loudest element
- Bass slightly below kick
- Set everything else relative to kick and bass
- Use a reference track for comparison

**2. EQ cleanup**
- High-pass everything that doesn't need sub-bass (synths, vocals, percussion)
- Cut mud (~200-400Hz) where it builds up
- Don't boost more than 3dB anywhere

**3. Panning**
- Kick, bass, snare: center
- Hi-hats: slightly off-center
- Percussion, synths: spread left and right for width
- Nothing hard-panned except for specific effects

**4. Compression**
- Bus compression on drums (reviewed in Lesson 3.9)
- Gentle compression on bass for consistency
- Light master bus compression (2:1, minimal gain reduction)

**5. Limiting**
- Put a limiter on the master channel
- Set ceiling to -0.3dB (prevents clipping)
- Aim for -8 to -6 LUFS loudness (typical for house)
- Don't slam the limiter — if you're pushing more than 3-4dB of gain reduction, your mix needs work

### Export settings
- Format: WAV (16-bit, 44.1kHz) for distribution
- WAV (24-bit, 44.1kHz or 48kHz) for mastering
- MP3 (320kbps) for sharing

### After exporting
- Listen on multiple systems (headphones, car, phone speaker)
- Compare loudness and tone to reference tracks
- Take notes on what to fix
- Don't aim for perfection — aim for finished

## Common Mistakes
- Tweaking forever instead of finishing
- Master too loud (squashed dynamics)
- Not checking on multiple playback systems

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Mix levels are balanced against a reference track
- [ ] Bass and kick are clean and defined
- [ ] Master peaks below 0dB
- [ ] Track has been exported and listened to on multiple systems

lessons.title: How to Reverse-Engineer a Track
lessons.description: Learn a systematic approach to analyzing any track.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Develop a systematic method for breaking down any house or tech house track into its components.

## Explanation
Reverse engineering is one of the fastest ways to learn. Instead of guessing how tracks are made, you systematically deconstruct them.

### The 6-step process

**Step 1: Listen passively (first play)**
- Just listen. Don't analyze. Feel the track.
- Note your emotional response. What grabs you?

**Step 2: Map the structure**
- Listen again with a stopwatch or your DAW
- Mark every section change (intro, build, drop, breakdown, outro)
- Count bars for each section
- Write it out: "Intro 16 bars → Build 8 bars → Drop 32 bars → ..."

**Step 3: Identify the elements**
- List every sound you can hear: kick, snare, hats, bass, synths, vocals, FX
- Note when each element enters and exits
- Which elements carry the main groove?

**Step 4: Analyze the sound design**
- What type of bass? (Sub, rolling, acid, stab)
- What type of synths? (Pad, lead, stab, pluck)
- Drum sounds: acoustic, electronic, layered?
- FX: reverb amount, delay, filtering

**Step 5: Study the mix**
- How loud is each element relative to the kick?
- How wide is the stereo image?
- Is there heavy sidechain pumping?
- Where does the energy peak?

**Step 6: What makes it work?**
- Why does this track grab you?
- What's the one thing that makes it stand out?
- What can you steal (technique, not melody) for your own music?

### Using DJ Lab's Track Analysis template
Open the Reverse-Engineering Lab and create a new analysis. Fill in each field as you work through the 6 steps.

## Common Mistakes
- Trying to analyze while casually listening (commit to focused listening)
- Not writing anything down (you'll forget)
- Only analyzing tracks you already know well

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have completed a full 6-step analysis of one track
- [ ] Structure is mapped with bar counts
- [ ] Sound elements are identified and described
- [ ] Have a clear answer to "what makes it work?"

lessons.title: Analyzing Structure & Arrangement
lessons.description: Map out sections, transitions, and arrangement choices in reference tracks.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Create detailed structural maps of house and tech house tracks, identifying arrangement patterns.

## Explanation
Structural analysis helps you understand **why** a track flows the way it does and gives you arrangement templates for your own productions.

### How to map structure
1. Load the track into your DAW at the correct BPM
2. Place markers at every section change
3. Label each section (intro, build, drop, breakdown, outro)
4. Count bars between markers

### What to look for

**Element density over time**:
- Draw a rough curve of how many elements are playing at each point
- This shows the energy arc of the track

**Transition techniques**:
- How does the artist move between sections?
- Filter sweeps? Drum fills? Silence? FX?
- How long are the transitions?

**The breakdown strategy**:
- What's removed during the breakdown?
- What new element is introduced?
- How long before the groove returns?

**Intro/outro design**:
- How long is the intro (in bars)?
- What elements are present in the intro?
- Is the outro a mirror of the intro?

### Structural patterns in tech house
Analyze 5+ tracks and you'll see patterns:
- Most intros: 16-32 bars, drums only
- Most drops: 32 bars
- Most breakdowns: 16-32 bars
- Total length: 5-7 minutes

These patterns are **conventions**, not rules. But knowing them helps you understand when an artist deliberately breaks them.

### Creating a template
Once you've analyzed 5+ tracks, create your own arrangement template based on the patterns you've found. Use it as a starting point for your productions.

## Common Mistakes
- Not counting bars accurately (recount to verify)
- Only analyzing one track (you need multiple to see patterns)
- Not noting transition techniques between sections

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have mapped the structure of at least 3 tracks
- [ ] Can identify common arrangement patterns
- [ ] Have noted transition techniques between sections
- [ ] Have created a personal arrangement template

lessons.title: Identifying Sound Design Elements
lessons.description: Recognize and describe synth types, bass sounds, and drum processing in tracks.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Listen to a track and accurately describe the sound design choices — what synths, bass types, and drum processing are used.

## Explanation
Training your ears to identify sound design elements is crucial for both DJing (understanding what makes tracks compatible) and production (recreating sounds you like).

### Bass identification
| Sound | Description | Example |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| Sub bass | Pure, deep, sine-wave feel | Minimal house |
| Rolling bass | Repeating pattern with filter movement | Tech house staple |
| Acid bass | Squelchy, resonant, 303-style | Acid house |
| Reese bass | Detuned saws, phasing, movement | Dark tech house |
| Stab bass | Short, punchy, rhythmic | Disco house |

### Synth identification
| Sound | Description | Example |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| Pad | Sustained, atmospheric, background | Breakdowns |
| Lead | Melodic, prominent, single notes | Hooks |
| Stab | Short chord hit, percussive | House drops |
| Pluck | Quick attack, short decay | Melodic tech house |
| Arp | Repeating ascending/descending pattern | Driving sections |

### Drum processing clues
- **Compressed/punchy kick**: Short, tight attack, professional sound
- **Room reverb on snare**: Sounds like it's in a physical space
- **Saturated hats**: Warm, crunchy top end
- **Layered clap**: Thick, wide, multiple sounds stacked

### Listening exercise
1. Pick a track
2. For each element you hear, describe it using the vocabulary above
3. Try to name the synthesis method (subtractive, FM, sample-based)
4. Note any processing you can hear (reverb, delay, distortion, filtering)

## Common Mistakes
- Using vague descriptions ("cool synth" instead of "filtered saw pad with long release")
- Not building vocabulary — use specific terms
- Only listening for elements you already know

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can identify bass type in any house track (sub, rolling, acid, etc.)
- [ ] Can describe synth sounds using proper terminology
- [ ] Can hear drum processing choices
- [ ] Have analyzed sound design in at least 3 tracks using DJ Lab

lessons.title: Studying Mix & FX Choices
lessons.description: Analyze reverb, delay, filtering, and spatial choices in professional tracks.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Identify and describe the mixing and effects decisions in a professional house track.

## Explanation
The mix is what makes a track sound professional. Learning to hear mix decisions helps you replicate them.

### Reverb analysis
- **How much reverb** is on each element? (dry, subtle, drenched)
- **What type?** (room, hall, plate)
- **Where is it used?** (claps usually have reverb, kicks usually don't)
- **Does reverb change** during the track? (more in breakdowns, less in drops)

### Delay analysis
- **What has delay?** (vocals, synth stabs)
- **What's the timing?** (1/8th, 1/4, dotted)
- **Is it subtle** (adds depth) or **obvious** (rhythmic effect)?
- **Ping-pong?** (bounces left-right)

### Filter automation
- **Where are filters used?** (builds, breakdowns, transitions)
- **Low-pass or high-pass?**
- **How fast** does the filter move?
- **Is resonance used** for emphasis?

### Stereo width
- **What's in the center?** (kick, bass, snare, vocals)
- **What's wide?** (hats, pads, synths, FX)
- **Does the width change** between sections? (narrow in drops, wide in breakdowns)

### Dynamic range
- **Is the mix compressed heavily** or does it breathe?
- **Is there sidechain pumping?** (bass ducking under kick)
- **How loud is the master?** Compare to references.

### FX spotting exercise
Listen to a track 5 times, each time focusing on ONE aspect:
1. Reverb only
2. Delay only
3. Filtering only
4. Stereo width only
5. Dynamics only

## Common Mistakes
- Trying to hear everything at once (focus on one aspect at a time)
- Not comparing to reference tracks (hard to judge in isolation)
- Confusing reverb with delay (reverb is diffuse, delay has distinct repeats)

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Can identify reverb types and amounts on different elements
- [ ] Can hear delay timing and placement
- [ ] Can describe the stereo image of a track
- [ ] Have completed a full mix analysis of at least 2 tracks

lessons.title: Building an Artist Sound Map
lessons.description: Document an artist's signature style, sounds, and techniques.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Create a comprehensive sound map of a house or tech house artist that captures their signature style.

## Explanation
An **artist sound map** is a reference document that captures everything distinctive about an artist's sound. It helps you understand what makes them unique and how to incorporate (not copy) their techniques.

### What to include

**1. Overview**
- Artist name, origin, active years
- Primary genre(s)
- Labels they release on
- One-sentence description of their sound

**2. Signature sounds**
- What makes them immediately recognizable?
- Recurring sound design choices
- Preferred synth types, bass sounds, drum textures
- Vocal treatment style (if applicable)

**3. Production techniques**
- How do they build tension?
- What's their arrangement style?
- How much do they use sampling?
- Mix characteristics (dry, wet, wide, narrow, loud, dynamic)

**4. Key tracks (3-5)**
For each track:
- What makes it a defining track for this artist?
- Link to your reverse-engineering analysis (if done)

**5. Evolution**
- How has their sound changed over time?
- Early work vs. recent work

**6. What to learn from them**
- What specific technique can you practice from studying this artist?
- What's the one thing they do better than anyone else?

### Example artists to study
- **Fisher**: Big bass, vocal chops, high energy tech house
- **CamelPhat**: Melodic tech house, atmospheric pads, vocal-driven
- **Patrick Topping**: Groovy, percussion-heavy, playful
- **Chris Lake**: Clean production, bass-driven, tight drums
- **Dom Dolla**: Disco-influenced, catchy, polished

### Using DJ Lab
Go to the Artist Sound Maps section and create a new entry. Use the template to fill in all fields.

## Common Mistakes
- Writing generic descriptions ("sounds good") instead of specific observations
- Only studying one track (you need 3-5 to identify patterns)
- Not noting what you can learn and apply

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have created a sound map for at least one artist
- [ ] Signature sounds are described with specific terminology
- [ ] 3-5 key tracks are listed with analysis
- [ ] Have identified at least one technique to practice from this artist

lessons.title: Recreating a Reference Track
lessons.description: Build a track inspired by a reference to deeply understand production techniques.
lessons.content_md:
## Objective
Recreate the essential elements of a reference track to internalize production techniques.

## Explanation
Recreation is the ultimate learning exercise. You're not stealing — you're studying by doing. The goal is to learn techniques, not to make a copy.

### The process

**Step 1: Choose your reference**
- Pick a track you've already analyzed in the Reverse-Engineering Lab
- Ideally one with a sound or technique you want to learn

**Step 2: Map the structure in your DAW**
- Create markers matching the reference track's structure
- Set your BPM to match
- This gives you a skeleton to build on

**Step 3: Recreate the drums**
- Find similar kick, snare, hat samples
- Program the same pattern
- Match the groove feel (swing amount, velocity)
- Don't try to be exact — close is fine

**Step 4: Recreate the bass**
- Identify the bass type (rolling, sub, acid, etc.)
- Design a similar bass patch
- Program a similar pattern and rhythm
- Apply sidechain to match the reference's pumping feel

**Step 5: Add the other elements**
- Synths, vocals, FX
- Focus on the technique, not the exact sound
- Use your own samples and presets

**Step 6: Arrange**
- Follow the reference's arrangement
- Match the element density at each section

**Step 7: Compare**
- A/B your recreation with the reference
- What sounds similar? What's different?
- Where are the biggest gaps in your skills?

### What you'll learn
- How hard it is to make things sound good (respect for the craft)
- Specific techniques you can reuse in original work
- Where your production skills need improvement
- The gap between "knowing about" a technique and "being able to do" it

### After recreation
- Don't release the recreation (it's a learning exercise)
- Take notes on what you learned
- Apply the techniques to an original track

## Common Mistakes
- Trying to make it perfect (aim for 80% similar, then move on)
- Getting stuck on one element (time-box each step to 30 minutes)
- Not comparing back to the reference regularly

## Success Checklist
- [ ] Have recreated the drum pattern of a reference track
- [ ] Have recreated a similar bass sound
- [ ] Have arranged the track to match the reference structure
- [ ] Can identify 3 specific things you learned from the process
- [ ] Have started an original track using one of the learned techniques

exercises.title: Map a Track's Structure
exercises.description: Pick any house track and write down every section (intro, breakdown, drop, outro) with timestamps. Identify at least 4 sections.

exercises.title: Count Bars in a Section
exercises.description: Play a house track and count the bars in the intro section. Verify by comparing with the waveform in your DJ software.

exercises.title: Count to 16
exercises.description: Play a house track and count bars out loud: '1-2-3-4, 2-2-3-4, 3-2-3-4...' up to 16. Clap on the first beat of each new 8-bar phrase. Do this 3 times.

exercises.title: Predict the Change
exercises.description: Play a track you don't know well. Count phrases and try to predict when the next section change will happen. Score yourself on 5 attempts.

exercises.title: Load and Play
exercises.description: Load a track onto each deck. Play Deck A, then Deck B. Practice pausing and cueing. Spend 10 minutes just getting comfortable with the controls.

exercises.title: Cue Preview Drill
exercises.description: Play Track A on speakers. Load Track B and preview it in your headphones using cue. Practice switching cue between decks. Set 3 cue points on Track B.

exercises.title: BPM Match Challenge
exercises.description: Load two tracks with different BPMs (within 3 BPM). Without looking at the BPM display, match them by ear. Time yourself. Repeat 5 times.

exercises.title: Sync On vs Off
exercises.description: Mix 3 tracks with sync ON, then mix the same 3 tracks with sync OFF. Note the differences in difficulty and result.

exercises.title: Level Matching
exercises.description: Load 5 different tracks and set each one's gain so it peaks at 0dB. Practice switching between them — the volume should feel consistent.

exercises.title: Bass Kill Drill
exercises.description: Play two tracks simultaneously. Cut the bass on Track B, blend it in, then swap the bass from A to B on a phrase boundary. Do this 5 times.

exercises.title: Clean Cut x5
exercises.description: Practice cutting between two tracks on phrase boundaries. Do 5 clean cuts. Each cut must land on beat 1 of a new phrase.

exercises.title: 16-Bar Fade
exercises.description: Fade from Track A to Track B over exactly 16 bars. Use channel faders and EQ. Record it and listen back.

exercises.title: Record & Review
exercises.description: Record a 15-minute practice mix. Listen back the next day. Note 3 things that went well and 3 things to improve. Log it in Practice Log.

exercises.title: Map 3 Tech House Tracks
exercises.description: Pick 3 tech house tracks. For each, write the full structure with bar counts. Compare the patterns you find.

exercises.title: Bass Swap Drill
exercises.description: Practice 10 bass swaps in a row between different track pairs. Each swap must be on a phrase boundary with no bass mud.

exercises.title: Loop & Mix
exercises.description: Loop the intro of an incoming track (8 bars). Hold the loop while you wait for the right phrase in the outgoing track. Exit the loop and complete the transition.

exercises.title: Filter Sweep Transition
exercises.description: Perform a high-pass filter sweep on Track A over 16 bars while bringing Track B in underneath. Record and review.

exercises.title: Energy-Rated Playlist
exercises.description: Rate 20 of your tracks on a 1-5 energy scale. Arrange them in an energy curve and plan a 30-minute set.

exercises.title: Library Cleanup
exercises.description: Organize 30 tracks with BPM, key, and energy level tags. Create 3 playlists: openers, peak, closers. Set cue points on all.

exercises.title: 30-Minute Mix
exercises.description: Plan and record a 30-minute mix. Write your track list and transition plan beforehand. Review the recording and note each transition's quality.

exercises.title: Echo Out Transition
exercises.description: Perform an echo-out transition: activate echo on Track A, fade it out while Track B takes over. The echo should tail off musically.

exercises.title: Camelot Matching
exercises.description: Tag 15 tracks with Camelot codes. Plan a 5-track sequence where each transition is within 1 step on the Camelot wheel.

exercises.title: Mock Live Set
exercises.description: Simulate a live set: prepare USB, plan first 3 tracks, play for 30 minutes without stopping. If a mix goes wrong, recover and keep going.

exercises.title: DAW Setup
exercises.description: Create a new project in your DAW. Set BPM to 125, create 4 tracks (kick, hats, bass, synth), and save the project.

exercises.title: 4-on-the-Floor Pattern
exercises.description: Program a 4-bar kick pattern with a kick on every beat. Choose a good kick sample, set velocity, and loop it. A/B with a reference track.

exercises.title: Full Drum Pattern
exercises.description: Build a complete drum pattern: kick + offbeat hi-hats + clap on 2&4 + one extra percussion element. It should groove on its own.

exercises.title: Swing A/B Test
exercises.description: Make two versions of your drum pattern: one straight, one with 55% swing on the hats. Listen to both. Which grooves more?

exercises.title: Sidechain Setup
exercises.description: Set up sidechain compression on a bass track triggered by the kick. Adjust attack and release until the bass pumps musically.

exercises.title: Rolling Bassline
exercises.description: Create a rolling bass patch (saw wave + filter envelope). Program an 8th-note pattern. Make it groove with the drums.

exercises.title: Full Arrangement
exercises.description: Take your loop and arrange it into a full track: 16-bar intro, build, drop, breakdown, drop 2, outro. Minimum 4 minutes.

exercises.title: Chop a Vocal
exercises.description: Find a royalty-free vocal sample. Chop it into 3-4 stabs. Pitch and time-stretch them to fit your track's BPM and key.

exercises.title: Compress the Drums
exercises.description: Apply compression to your kick (slow attack, medium release) and bus compression to all drums. Compare before/after.

exercises.title: Layer a Kick
exercises.description: Create a layered kick from 2 samples: a sub kick (low thump) and a top kick (click). EQ each to occupy different ranges. Combine them.

exercises.title: Build a Buildup
exercises.description: Create a 16-bar build using at least 3 techniques: riser, snare roll, and filter automation. It should make the drop feel impactful.

exercises.title: Export & Review
exercises.description: Export your finished track as WAV. Listen on headphones, speakers, and phone. Take notes on what sounds different on each system.

exercises.title: Full Track Analysis
exercises.description: Pick a house or tech house track you love. Complete the full 6-step analysis process and save it in DJ Lab's Reverse-Engineering Lab.

exercises.title: Structure Comparison
exercises.description: Map the structure of 3 tracks by the same artist. Compare the patterns. Write down the arrangement template they tend to follow.

exercises.title: Sound Identification Quiz
exercises.description: Listen to 5 different tracks. For each, identify and describe: bass type, main synth type, and one notable processing effect. Use specific terminology.

exercises.title: Mix Breakdown
exercises.description: Pick one track and listen to it 5 times, each time focusing on: (1) reverb, (2) delay, (3) filtering, (4) stereo width, (5) dynamics. Write findings for each.

exercises.title: Artist Sound Map
exercises.description: Choose a house/tech house artist. Create a complete sound map in DJ Lab with signature sounds, key tracks, and production notes.

exercises.title: Reference Recreation
exercises.description: Recreate the drums and bass of a reference track in your DAW. Spend 2 hours maximum. Compare with the original and note 3 things you learned.
